title: BUG: test_assignment_not_inplace incorrectly xfailed due to wrong assertion
body:
@jbrockmendel asked [claude] to open this.

## Summary

`tests/computation/test_eval.py::TestOperations::test_assignment_not_inplace` is marked `xfail` with reason `"Unknown: Omitted test_ in name prior."` The test was previously named without a `test_` prefix so pytest never collected it. When it was renamed, it started failing — but the failure is due to a bug **in the test itself**, not in pandas.

## The bug

The test checks that `df.eval("c = a + b", inplace=False)` does **not** modify `df` in place. However, the final assertion compares `df` (2 columns) against `expected` (3 columns, including `"c"`):

```python
actual = df.eval("c = a + b", inplace=False)
expected = df.copy()
expected["c"] = expected["a"] + expected["b"]
tm.assert_frame_equal(df, expected)  # wrong: compares `df` instead of `actual`
```

This assertion would only pass if `df` *was* modified in place — the exact bug the test was meant to guard against (GH#9297).

## Fix

- Remove the `xfail` marker
- Replace `tm.assert_frame_equal(df, expected)` with `tm.assert_frame_equal(actual, expected)`
- Add a check that `df` is unchanged, e.g. `assert list(df.columns) == ["a", "b"]`

```
git fetch upstream
```

2. The second part of the issue is that when the typo is fixed, the first line becomes redundant, since the second line fetches everything the first one fetches and also fetches the tags.

One can replace the two lines above with a single one without typos and achieve the same result
```
git fetch upstream --tags`
```

title: BUG: unique().item() query no longer possible since unique() method no longer returns array
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
pd.__version__
# '3.0.0'
df = pd.DataFrame([
  {"person": "John", "userName": "Johnny1234"}, 
  {"person": "Jane", "userName": "Jane3"}
])
person = df.query("userName == 'Johnny1234'")['person'].unique().item()

# Traceback (most recent call last):
#   File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
# AttributeError: 'ArrowStringArray' object has no attribute 'item
```

### Issue Description

`unique` series method now returns array type rather than a series of unique items, breaking the use of .unique().item(), see discussions https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/18262#issuecomment-546746982 and https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/29250

Previously the use of the method would allow one to query a column with the expectation that only one result was returned. If none or more were returned, .item() would return a value error. 

The workaround for now is to do rewrap the array in a series object

```
person = pd.Series(df.query("userName == 'Johnny1234'")['person'].unique()).item()
```

### Expected Behavior

We would expect the following response
```
# 'John'
```

title: PERF: Avoid drop_duplicates(keep=False) in DataFrame.__getitem__ for single-column access
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

Observed (before fix): With n = 1000000 columns, 1000 accesses can take on the order of several seconds because each access builds a new Index via drop_duplicates(keep=False).

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/frame.py#L4162-L4169


```code
import pandas as pd
import timeit

# DataFrame with many columns and duplicate names; one column "key" appears once
n = 1000000
cols = ["a"] * (n - 1) + ["key"]
df = pd.DataFrame(0, index=range(10000), columns=cols)


# Repeated single-column access (e.g. in a loop or pipeline)
def access():
    for _ in range(100):
        _ = df["key"]


# Current state: each df["key"] calls columns.drop_duplicates(keep=False) → O(n) + allocation

sec = timeit.timeit(access, number=10)
print(f"1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): {sec:.2f}s")
```

Output

```
1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): 8.69s
```

Expected: Single-column access when the key appears once should not rebuild the Index on every access; runtime should be much lower (e.g. well under 1 second for 1000 accesses).

Suggested Fix

```
if not is_mi:
    try:
        loc = self.columns.get_loc(key)
        if isinstance(loc, int):
            return self._get_item(key)
    except (KeyError, InvalidIndexError):
        pass
elif is_mi and self.columns.is_unique and key in self.columns:
    return self._getitem_multilevel(key)
```

Output would be

```
1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): 0.04s
```

body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
examples=['ga',
          'Áa',
          '永a',
          '🐍a']
for t in examples:
    objects = pd.Series([t], dtype=object)
    strs = pd.Series([t], dtype=str)
    print('python:', t.find('a'), 
          'pandas with object type:', objects.str.find('a')[0],
          'pandas with string type:', strs.str.find('a')[0],          
          )
```

### Issue Description

`str.find` appears to be indexing its result based on bytes rather than characters. In the example, the basic python `str` type, and a `Series` using the `object` `dtype`, `find('a')` is `1` for all the example strings, as expected. With a `Series` using the new `str` `dtype`, the result is 1, 2, 3, and 4 respectively. Note that encoded in UTF-8, Á takes two bytes, 永 takes three, and 🐍 takes four, so I suspect it's counting bytes instead of characters. `len` gives a result of 2 regardless of dtype.

The result of `str.find` shouldn't change depending on dtype.

body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I suggest `pd.case_when` to support `pd.col` expression - the expression can be evaluated to either booleans or expected output within the case_when function : 

```py
data = {'name': ['Jason', 'Molly', 'Tina', 'Jake', 'Amy'], 
        'age': [42, 52, 36, 24, 73], 
        'preTestScore': [4, 24, 31, 2, 3],
        'postTestScore': [25, 94, 57, 62, 70]}
df = pd.DataFrame(data, columns = ['name', 'age', 'preTestScore', 'postTestScore'])
df
    name  age  preTestScore  postTestScore
0  Jason   42             4             25
1  Molly   52            24             94
2   Tina   36            31             57
3   Jake   24             2             62
4    Amy   73             3             70

caselist=[(pd.col('age').lt(10), 'baby'), 
          (pd.col('age').ge(10) & pd.col('age').lt(20), 'kid'), 
          (df.age.ge(20) & df.age.lt(30), 'young'), 
          (df.age.ge(30) & df.age.lt(50), 'mature'), 
          (df.age.ge(50), 'grandpa')]

df.assign(elderly = df.age.case_when(caselist=caselist))
    name  age  preTestScore  postTestScore  elderly
0  Jason   42             4             25   mature
1  Molly   52            24             94  grandpa
2   Tina   36            31             57   mature
3   Jake   24             2             62    young
4    Amy   73             3             70  grandpa
```

### Feature Description

within the `case_when` code, the pd.col expression is evaluated on the current dataframe, everything else stays as is

### Alternative Solutions

there isn't an alternative option at the moment. using pd.col makes things a bit cleaner. We can also leave things as is.

title: ENH: Allow merge to override columns
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I wish that merge would be able to solve column name conflicts by allowing to override one value. This is especially useful for jupyter notebooks when I have cells that perform a pd.merge() and have the resulting df be the same variable as one of the inputs:

```python
df = pd.merge(df, otherdf, **otherargs)
```

If I rerun a cell containing such a merge, the dataframe columns are changed. There are two possible workarounds, the first is to just never assign to the same name, the other one is this:

```python
df = pd.merge(df.loc[:,~df.columns.isin(otherdf.columns), otherdf, **otherargs)
```

### Feature Description

Add a new parameter to the pd.merge() function to allow overriding columns:

```python
def merge(left, right, override: str | None=None, **kwargs):
    """
    Parameters
    ----------
    override: {"left","right",None}
        default: None
        If not None suffix will be ignored and the columns of the specified dataframe
        will override the other one in case of a conflict
    """
```

### Alternative Solutions

Alternatively override could be a bool and it will always override the left dataframe

### Additional Context

I am happy to make a pull request if you are okay with having this feature included

title: DOC: Intersphinx references to common items break on latest docs
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that the issue still exists on the latest versions of the docs on `main` [here](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/)


### Location of the documentation

https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/objects.inv

### Documentation problem

Since the release of pandas 3.0.0, our documentation-building CI (using sphinx autodoc) stopped recognising simple classes like `pd.DataFrame` and `pd.Index` as valid targets in the pandas documentation, which broke the automatically generated class links (documented in https://github.com/aertslab/CREsted/issues/181). 
```
<unknown>:1: WARNING: py:class reference target not found: pandas.core.indexes.base.Index [ref.class]
<unknown>:1: WARNING: py:class reference target not found: pandas.core.frame.DataFrame [ref.class]
<unknown>:1: WARNING: py:class reference target not found: pandas.core.frame.DataFrame [ref.class]
<unknown>:1: WARNING: py:class reference target not found: pandas.core.frame.DataFrame [ref.class]
<unknown>:1: WARNING: py:class reference target not found: pandas.core.frame.DataFrame [ref.class]
<unknown>:1: WARNING: py:class reference target not found: pandas.core.frame.DataFrame [ref.class]
```
(In our case, since we build the docs strictly, this even prevents from building them altogether.) These warnings are from type hints (to normal `pd.DataFrame`/`pd.Index`) that would normally be turned into links to the `pd.DataFrame`/`pd.Index` docs, and indeed worked fine up to 2 weeks ago.

This seems to be related to the change of the `__module__` attribute. As shown in the warnings above, on pandas 2.x, `pd.DataFrame`'s `__module__` is used, and it's automatically expanded to `pandas.core.frame.DataFrame`. This is then requested to the pandas docs, which previously resolved this back to `pandas.DataFrame`. See for example the DataFrame link [here](https://crested.readthedocs.io/en/latest/api/tools/_autosummary/crested.tl.modisco.create_pattern_tf_dict.html). However, since the release of 3.0.0, this is no longer available in the stable (or dev) docs:

```
> uvx sphobjinv suggest -u https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/objects.inv pandas.core.frame.DataFrame
Project: pandas
Version: 3.0.0
No results found with score at/above current threshold of 75.

> uvx sphobjinv suggest -u https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/2.3/objects.inv pandas.core.frame.DataFrame
Project: pandas
Version: 2.3.3
1 result found at/above current threshold of 75.
:py:class:`pandas.core.frame.DataFrame`
```

That means any sphinx documentation building that isn't already running on pandas 3.0.0 will automatically resolve `pd.DataFrame` to `pandas.core.frame.DataFrame`, and their link to the pandas documentation will break.
We can fix this problem locally by changing the pandas docs location from https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/ to https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/version/2.3/, but this keeps the references always pointing to outdated pandas docs, which I don't think is a preferable situation.

### Suggested fix for documentation

Is it possible to add aliases to pandas' sphinx objects list to accept the old definition paths and point them to the new public-facing names?

While following the documentation, I copied an example code snippet directly into my notebook. However, the snippet includes Python REPL prompt symbols (>>>), which causes errors when pasted as regular code.
Example from the docs:

```
>>> s = pd.Series({"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3})
>>> s.size
3
```
The `>>>` symbols appear to be REPL prompts, but this is not explicitly stated. Removing them manually is required for the code to run, which may be confusing, especially for beginners.

### Suggested fix for documentation

I suggest one of the following:
 
- Remove `>>>` from copyable code blocks, or

- Clearly label the snippet as Python REPL output, or

- Provide a version of the example that can be copied and pasted directly.

title: BUG: `pd.read_hdf` unable to retrieve a pd.Series with dtype as "datetime64" since v3.0.0
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path

pd.read_hdf(Path("path_to_old_store"), key="datetime_data_exported_via_to_hdf_in_earlier_pandas_version")
```

### Issue Description

From pandas 3.0.0 an error occurs when retrieving via `pd.read_hdf` a `pd.Series` with dtype as "datetime64", i.e. older data that was saved via `pd.to_hdf` before (I imagine) pandas started writing datetime64 units.

It seems that the equivalent situation for "timedelta64" is accommodated for by [this if clause](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/8ff98463033bd413dabdb5036a92744de2d31fe4/pandas/io/pytables.py#L3095) which sets the default unit to 'ns' in the event that the dtype is merely "timedelta64". However, for "datetime64" the dtype is passed through to `_set_tz` which in turn gets the unit [here](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/8ff98463033bd413dabdb5036a92744de2d31fe4/pandas/io/pytables.py#L5108) from `np.datetime_data` which returns the unit of a "datetime64" dtype as 'generic'. This 'generic' value ends up being passed to the 'unit' parameter of `DatetimeTZDtype` and that function throws an error as a `TimeUnit` is expected, i.e. one of "s", "ms", "us", "ns".

I'm not sure if this is a bug or rather a matter of `pd.read_hdf` in Pandas 3.0.0 not being backwards compatible with data exported from earlier versions? The fact that the equivalent situation for 'timedelta64' appears to have been accommodated seems to suggest it's a bug...?

Might the fix be as simple as including the following to immediately follow [pytables.py L3090](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/8ff98463033bd413dabdb5036a92744de2d31fe4/pandas/io/pytables.py#L3089):
```python
if dtype == "datetime64":
	dtype = "datetime64[ns]"
```
?

Cheers
Marcus

### Expected Behavior

For data imported via `pd.read_hdf` would have expected pandas 3.0.0 to infer datetime resolution where not otherwise defined.

title: ENH: Allow `np.ndarray` in `check_result_array` for certain `dtype`
body:
### Feature Type

- [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Aggregations are using `check_result_array` to verify that the aggregation operation reduced the dimension. To do so it checks that the given `obj` is not a `np.ndarray` and if so the expected `dtype` is at least `object`. The expected `dtype` hereby is the `dtype` of the `group` before the aggregation. This can be an issue if the actual aggregated `obj` is expected to still be an `np.ndarray` but the expected `dtype` is not `object`.

`_aggregate_series_pure_python` calls `check_result_array(res, group.dtype)` to verify result of aggregation:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/433b140936aadec0f42c46e4e827f6f545569bbc/pandas/core/groupby/ops.py#L986-L1005

`check_result_array`:
https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/433b140936aadec0f42c46e4e827f6f545569bbc/pandas/core/groupby/ops.py#L81-L89

### Feature Description

The `dtype` parameter in `check_result_array` lets us know what the `dtype` of the `group` was. As far as I know every `dtype` has the `type` property that specifies of which type a singular element of an `array` with this `dtype` would be. Consider the following example:
```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1,1,2], "B": [10,20,30]})
>>> df
   A   B
0  1  10
1  1  20
2  2  30
>>> df.dtypes
A    int64
B    int64
dtype: object
>>> grouped = df.groupby("A").agg("first")
>>> grouped
    B
A
1  10
2  30
>>> grouped.dtypes
B    int64
dtype: object
>>> grouped["B"].dtype
dtype('int64')
>>> type(grouped["B"].iloc[0]) == df["B"].dtype.type
True
```
The `type` of an element of the aggregation result (here "`first"` function) is the same as the `dtype.type` of the original column `df["B"]`.

In my opinion the same should be true for other `dtypes`. Therefore if this `dtype.type` is an `np.ndarray` then `check_result_array` should not raise a `ValueError` as it is likely that the aggregation still worked as expected.

Such a check could be implemented with:
```python
isinstance(obj, dtype.type)
```

Or in the full function (description still would have to be updated to accommodate the change):
```python
 def check_result_array(obj, dtype) -> None: 
     # Our operation is supposed to be an aggregation/reduction. If 
     #  it returns an ndarray, this likely means an invalid operation has 
     #  been passed. See test_apply_without_aggregation, test_agg_must_agg 
     if isinstance(obj, np.ndarray): 
         if dtype != object or isinstance(obj, dtype.type): 
             # If it is object dtype, the function can be a reduction/aggregation 
             #  and still return an ndarray e.g. test_agg_over_numpy_arrays 
             raise ValueError("Must produce aggregated value") 
```

### Alternative Solutions

Not sure if there are alternative solutions.

### Additional Context

I stumbled on the issue during my tests, specifically `BaseGroupbyTests::test_groupby_agg_extension` which calls `first` as the aggregation function, of the Astropy ExtensionArray that I am currently writing. Its main feature is the support of Astropy `Quantity` objects that support physical units and are themselve a subclass of `np.ndarray`. Therefore `check_result_array` fails as the result of an aggregation can be a `zerodim` `Quantity` object, which is not scalar but still a `np.ndarray`

All other issues I found about `check_result_array` seem to be related to `pd.Series.mode` as this aggregation can also create arrays as a result if there are more than one mode:
- https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/38534

title: BUG: groupby with observed=False assigns rows with NaN categorical keys to wrong groups
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
print("pandas version", pd.__version__, "\n")


# Reproduction focuses on: groupby(observed=False) + categorical key with NaN

# sample DataFrame
df = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "metric": [10.0, 5.0, 12.0, 20.0, 8.0],
        "sector": [1, 2, 1, 2, np.nan],
    },
    index=pd.MultiIndex.from_tuples(
        [
            ("2026-01-01", "A"),
            ("2026-01-01", "B"),
            ("2026-02-01", "A"),
            ("2026-02-01", "B"),
            ("2026-02-01", "C"),
        ],
        names=["dates", "company"],
    ),
)

# make df["sector"] categorical
df["sector"] = pd.Categorical(df["sector"], categories=[1, 2], ordered=True)
print("Input Dataframe:\n", df, "\n")

# group by date and sector
print("Group membership:\n")
grouped = df.groupby(["dates", "sector"], observed=False)
for k, v in grouped.groups.items():
    print(k, list(v))

# compute sum of group values
print("\nSum over groups:\n")
g_sum = df.groupby(["dates", "sector"], observed=False)["metric"].sum()
print(g_sum)
```

### Issue Description

In pandas 3.0.0, `DataFrame.groupby` seems to incorrectly assigns rows whose grouping key is a Categorical containing NaN to non-NaN groups when grouping by multiple keys with `observed=False`.

This results in:
- incorrect group membership (`DataFrame.groupby.groups`)
- incorrect aggregation results (e.g. `DataFrame.groupby.sum()`)

The same code produces correct results in pandas 2.3.3, so this appears to be a regression.

### Expected Behavior

Using pandas 3.0.0, the reproducible example above yields:

```
pandas version 3.0.0 

Input Dataframe:
                     metric sector
dates      company               
2026-01-01 A          10.0      1
           B           5.0      2
2026-02-01 A          12.0      1
           B          20.0      2
           C           8.0    NaN 

Group membership:

('2026-01-01', 1) [('2026-01-01', 'A')]
('2026-01-01', 2) [('2026-01-01', 'B'), ('2026-02-01', 'C')]
('2026-02-01', 1) [('2026-02-01', 'A')]
('2026-02-01', 2) [('2026-02-01', 'B')]

Sum over groups:

dates       sector
2026-01-01  1         10.0
            2         13.0
2026-02-01  1         12.0
            2         20.0
Name: metric, dtype: float64
```

The row `('2026-02-01', 'C')]` has `sector = NaN` and should not belong to a group with category `1` or `2`. It is however incorrectly assigned to the group `('2026-01-01', 2.0)` as shown in the group membership. The sum over the group `('2026-01-01', 2.0)` yields a value of `8 + 5 = 13` although a value of `5` is expected.

In contrast, using pandas 2.3.3, the reproducible example above yields the expected behavior:

```
pandas version 2.3.3 

Input Dataframe:
                     metric sector
dates      company               
2026-01-01 A          10.0      1
           B           5.0      2
2026-02-01 A          12.0      1
           B          20.0      2
           C           8.0    NaN 

Group membership:

('2026-01-01', 1.0) [('2026-01-01', 'A')]
('2026-01-01', 2.0) [('2026-01-01', 'B')]
('2026-02-01', 1.0) [('2026-02-01', 'A')]
('2026-02-01', 2.0) [('2026-02-01', 'B')]
('2026-02-01', nan) [('2026-02-01', 'C')]

Sum over groups:

dates       sector
2026-01-01  1         10.0
            2          5.0
2026-02-01  1         12.0
            2         20.0
Name: metric, dtype: float64
```

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame([["x", 1], [np.nan, 2]], columns=["a", "b"])
grouped = df.groupby("a", dropna=False)
```

### Issue Description

On the latest Pandas 2.x version (2.3), performing a `groupby(dropna=False)` and then attempting to access `DataFrameGroupBy.groups` property results in the following exception:

title: BUG: Pandas converts nullable int to float, even when this loses data
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
def add_two(x):
    if pd.isna(x):
        return pd.NA
    return x+2

sequence = [10000000000000001,None] #above the float integer precision limit
df1 = pd.DataFrame(sequence, dtype='Int64')
df1[0] = df1[0].apply(add_two).astype('Int64')
print(int(df1[0][0])) # 002, not 003
```

### Issue Description

Anytime there's a null value in a series when using .apply() (or creating a dataframe with no dtype specified), it will be converted to a float, even if the data type it already is can support null values, and is a better fit for the data, and this results in loss of precision compared to not converting

Possibly related to https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/62710

### Expected Behavior

Pandas should not convert data types to a float when this loses data and is a worse fit for the data.

### Pandas version checks

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
```

title: BUG: Handling of `None` column name in `from_records()` is now all-NaN instead of values
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

dict_data = [
    {'fieldA': 'X', 'fieldB': 'Y', None: ['1000']},
    {'fieldA': 'Z', 'fieldB': '', None: ['900']}
]

pd.DataFrame.from_records(dict_data)
```

### Issue Description

Using that example list-of-dicts, which is the result of an incorrect CSV file read with `csv.DictReader()`:

On Pandas 3.0.0, the output just has a **NaN column name** with **NaN values**, which doesn't seem useful.:
```
  fieldA fieldB  NaN
0      X      Y  NaN
1      Z         NaN
```

Even if that last field was not an array, and just `None: '1000'` and `None: '900'`, the result is still the same NaN column name with NaN values.
 

### Expected Behavior

It should have `None` as the column name and the values should be present.

While it may be more consistent with the behaviour of the `columns` param of DataFrame.from_records() _"(any names not found in the data will become all-NA columns)"_ - the column name is already different and it's a breaking change wrt how this used to be handled when no column param is provided:

On version 2.3.3, the result of that same code is:
```
  fieldA fieldB    None
0      X      Y  [1000]
1      Z          [900]
```

which can be used to inform the end user of the missing header/extra column. When it's NaN _name and values_, nothing can done with it except to inform the end user "there probably an extra column".

title: BUG: AttributeError: 'ArrowStringArray' object has no attribute 'item'
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# Pandas object that contains only 1 unique value:
s = pd.Series(["foo", "foo"])
s.unique()
# pandas 2.3.3:
# array(['foo'], dtype=object)
#
# pandas 3.0.0:
# <ArrowStringArray>
# ['foo']
# Length: 1, dtype: str

# Retrieve the unique value as a scalar
s.astype(object).unique().item()
# pandas 2.3.3 or 3.0.0: 'foo'

# Retrieve the unique value as a scalar
s.unique().item():
# pandas 2.3.3: 'foo'
# pandas 3.0.0: AttributeError: 'ArrowStringArray' object has no attribute 'item'
```

### Issue Description

In pandas 2.3.3 and earlier `(...).unique().item()` worked as a way to get a single unique value that appeared in a Series —or DataFrame column, or as the result of other operation that resulted in a Series. This was concise and preferable to, for instance, `(...).unique()[0]` because it would raise an exception if earlier code produced a *non*-unique Series.

With pandas 3.0.0, when the dtype of the Series is `str`, the result of `.unique()` is ArrowStringArray, which [lacks an `.item()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.arrays.ArrowStringArray.html).

If this is a deliberate breaking change, then I would expect that (a) it would be mentioned in [the relevant section of the release notes](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/whatsnew/v3.0.0.html#other-api-changes); and/or (b) version < 3.0.0 would give some kind of DeprecationWarning to draw attention to expected breakage with the release of 3.0.0. As far as I can tell, neither of these happened.

### Expected Behavior

The example above gives `'foo'` on the last line with pandas 3.0.0—same as with pandas 2.3.3.

title: ENH: Data Entropy & Information Loss Tracking for DataFrame Transformations
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Pandas does not provide any method to measure the information loss which occurs when DataFrame transformations are applied. 

Data resolution decreases permanently through common operations because users cannot observe this reduction which results from rounding and binning and aggregation and encoding and filtering and deduplication. Users create data compression that exceeds proper limits which leads to the loss of valuable information without their awareness. 

I want pandas to provide users with information loss measurements which show how transformations affect data processing because this will help them choose preprocessing methods and identify excessive operations which will improve their data pipeline trust.

### Feature Description

The system will start tracking operational data transformations through its mandatory tracking system which will record every DataFrame transformation that occurs. 

The feature would:

- The system will calculate entropy values at the column level using Shannon entropy for discrete data and histogram-based entropy for continuous data.

- The system will measure information loss through its normalized entropy difference calculation which compares two different states.

- The system will track information loss from operations that occur within a monitoring environment.

Example API:
       with df.track_information() as info:
           df["price"] = df["price"].round(0)
           df["age_group"] = pd.cut(df["age"], bins=5)

        info.report()

Conceptual implementation

      def entropy(series):
          if is_discrete(series):
              p = value_counts(series) / len(series)
              return -sum(p * log2(p))
          else:
               bins = adaptive_bins(series)
               p = histogram(series, bins) / len(series)
               return -sum(p * log2(p))


The system performs lazy entropy calculations which apply to specific columns that undergo changes. The system applies adaptive binning to continuous data in order to produce consistent estimation results. The system calculates dataset-level information loss by summing all column-specific information losses. The feature requires user activation because it creates no performance impact until the user decides to use it. The system enables users to monitor DataFrame transformation impacts on information content while maintaining the original pandas functional behavior.



### Alternative Solutions

Multiple different methods exist as potential alternatives for evaluation. 

Relying on documentation or user discipline Users would need to decide how much information they lost through their transformation work. The current system proves unmanageable because it creates errors while users cannot track the total impact which develops throughout their different workflows.

Heuristic warnings for specific operations Pandas should develop a system which generates alerts about dangerous functions which include binning and rounding as destructive actions. The system would operate at a broad level but its results would not show the actual information loss degree which occurs through a specific dataset.

Downstream model metrics (e.g., feature importance, performance) The model behavior permits users to infer information loss yet this method only works during the machine learning stage and it does not serve general data analysis or reporting purposes.

External profiling or data quality tools Existing tools examine missing data and data distribution patterns and schema validation processes, but they lack the ability to monitor how data transformations create information loss which they can trace back to particular processes.

The available alternatives failed to meet requirements because they lacked the ability to show information loss which occurs during pandas operations at both direct and transformation-level contexts.

### Additional Context

_No response_

title: BUG: Inconsistent BOM handling in pd.read_csv with encoding='utf-8'
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import io

# CSV with UTF‑8 BOM
bytes_data = b"\xef\xbb\xbfName,Age\nJohn,25"
bio = io.BytesIO(bytes_data)


df_c = pd.read_csv(bio, encoding="utf-8")
print(repr(df_c.columns[0]))  # 'Name'

bio.seek(0)
# but different behaviour in text wrapper
stream = io.TextIOWrapper(bio, encoding='utf-8')

print(repr(stream.read())) # '\ufeffName,Age\nJohn,25'

```

### Issue Description

When reading a UTF-8 encoded CSV that contains a BOM, specifying `encoding='utf-8'` pandas strips the BOM from the first column header and textwrapper leaves it as an invisible `\ufeff` character. The outcome depends on the parsing, but this behaviour is undocumented and inconsistent.

### Expected Behavior

I expected `encoding='utf-8'` either to always keep the BOM (requiring `utf-8-sig` to remove it) or to always strip it, regardless of parser. At minimum, the documentation should clarify how BOMs are handled across engines when using `encoding='utf-8'`.

title: BUG: `DataFrame.from_records` ignores exclude argument when `nrows=0`
body:

### Reproducible Example

```python
from pandas import DataFrame
# Create sample data
rows = [
    {"a": 1, "b": 2, "c": 3},
    {"a": 4, "b": 5, "c": 6},
    {"a": 7, "b": 8, "c": 9},
]

result = DataFrame.from_records(
           iter(rows), columns=["a", "b", "c"], exclude = ["b"], nrows=0
       )

assert (result.columns == ["a", "c"]).all(), "Column exclusion did not work as expected"
```

### Issue Description

In Pandas 2.3.3, `result.columns` was empty when `nrows=0`. This issue was reported in Issue #61140 and fixed in #62085. However, this PR seem to accidentally cause regression in which DataFrame.from_records ignored `exclude` argument. In Pandas 3.0.0rc2, result.columns will be ["a", "b", "c"] and do not exclude ["b"]

### Expected Behavior

### Reproducible Example

Using `groupby.agg` with a named aggregation which doesn't actually use relabeling is much slower (for small dfs) than the same operation without a named aggregation

```python
   ...:     # Random number of users and values
```

title: BUG: str methods fail with regex backreferences on PyArrow dtype
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.
### Issue Description
#### Backreferences Also Affected by RE2 Limitations

The PyArrow string backend uses the RE2 regex engine, which does not support backreferences (e.g., \1, \2, \3). Currently, using str.contains() and other string methods with backreference patterns raises a raw pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid error.
This is related to but distinct from issue https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/60833 (lookarounds) and PR https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/63613, which handle lookaround assertions. Backreferences are a separate regex feature that also fails with RE2.
As PyArrow becomes the default backend in pandas 3.0, this will cause regressions for users relying on backreferences in regex patterns.
### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

# Create Series with PyArrow dtype (will be default in pandas 3.0)
s = pd.Series(['hello hello', 'world world', 'foo bar'], dtype='string[pyarrow]')

# Pattern using backreference \1 to match repeated words
# This works with Python's re module but fails with RE2
try:
    result = s.str.contains(r'(\w+)\s\1', regex=True)
    print(result)
except Exception as e:
    print(f"Error: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
```
Actual Behavior
Raises a cryptic error:
```
ArrowInvalid: Invalid regular expression: invalid escape sequence: \1
```
No guidance on:

- Why this fails (RE2 limitation)
- How to fix it (use different dtype or rewrite pattern)
- Alternative approaches

### Expected Behavior
Ideal: Automatic fallback to Python regex engine when backreferences are detected (similar to PR #63613 for lookarounds)
Minimum: Clear, actionable error message:
```
ValueError: Pattern contains backreference '\1' which is not supported by 
PyArrow's RE2 engine.

Solutions:
  - Use dtype="string[python]" for full regex support
  - Rewrite pattern to avoid backreferences
  
RE2 syntax reference: https://github.com/google/re2/wiki/Syntax
```

Works fine with object dtype:
```python
pythons_obj = pd.Series(['hello hello', 'world world', 'foo bar'], dtype='object')
result = s_obj.str.contains(r'(\w+)\s\1', regex=True)
# Returns: [True, True, False]  ✅
```
### RE2 Limitation
According to [RE2 syntax documentation](https://github.com/google/re2/wiki/Syntax), RE2 doesn't support:

- ✅ Lookarounds (handled by this PR): (?<=...), (?=...), (?<!...), (?!...)
- ❌ Backreferences (not handled): \1, \2, \3, etc.
- ❌ Named backreferences: (?P=name)

### Suggested Fix
Extend _has_regex_lookaround() to detect backreferences as well. The method could be renamed to something like _has_unsupported_re2_features().
Looking at the [re._parser source](https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/main/Lib/re/_parser.py), backreferences use the GROUPREF opcode, so detection would be:
```python
@staticmethod
def _has_unsupported_re2_features(pat: str | re.Pattern) -> bool:
    """Check if pattern contains features unsupported by RE2 engine."""
    try:
        from re import _parser
        
        str_pat = pat.pattern if isinstance(pat, re.Pattern) else pat
        tokens = _parser.parse(str_pat)
        
        # Check for lookarounds (current implementation)
        if any(op_code in [_parser.ASSERT_NOT, _parser.ASSERT] 
               for op_code, _ in tokens):
            return True
        
        # Check for backreferences (new)
        if any(op_code == _parser.GROUPREF 
               for op_code, _ in tokens):
            return True
            
        return False
    except Exception:
        # If detection fails, be conservative and don't fallback
        return False
```
### Testing
I can help add test cases for backreferences if this approach looks good!
### Installed Versions

<details> 

Python: 3.11.14
Pandas: 0+untagged.36847.g27935d8.dirty (dev main)
PyArrow: 22.0.0

</details>
**Note:** Issue also reproduces on pandas 2.2.0+ with PyArrow 15.0.0+.

 I have confirmed this bug exists on the main branch of pandas.


Issue Description
The PyArrow string backend uses the RE2 regex engine, which does not support backreferences (e.g., \1, \2, \3). Currently, using str.contains() and other string methods with backreference patterns raises a raw pyarrow.lib.ArrowInvalid error.

    print(result)

Actual Behavior
Raises a cryptic error:
ArrowInvalid: Invalid regular expression: invalid escape sequence: \1

Why this fails (RE2 limitation)
How to fix it (use different dtype or rewrite pattern)
Alternative approaches

Ideal: Automatic fallback to Python regex engine when backreferences are detected (similar to PR #63613 for lookarounds)
Minimum: Clear, actionable error message:
ValueError: Pattern contains backreference '\1' which is not supported by 
PyArrow's RE2 engine.

# Output: 0     True
#         1     True
#         2    False
# dtype: bool

Similar to PR #63613 (which handles lookarounds), pandas should:
Option 1: Auto-fallback (Recommended)

Detect backreferences in regex patterns using re._parser
Automatically fall back to Python regex engine
Optionally warn users about performance implications

Option 2: Better Error Messages (Quick Win)

Catch ArrowInvalid when backreferences are detected
Provide clear, actionable error message with workarounds

Implementation hint: The re._parser.GROUPREF opcode identifies backreferences, similar to how ASSERT/ASSERT_NOT identify lookarounds.

❌ Backreferences: This issue - \1, \2, (?P=name)
❌ Conditional patterns: (?(id)yes|no)

#63613 - PR implementing auto-fallback for lookarounds

title: Cleanup: Add type: ignore comments for comparison-overlap in datetimes.py
body:
## Description

Following up on #58475, which was closed after the team decided against 
implementing type-safe constructors for `Timestamp`/`Timedelta`.

While that decision is sound, it leaves some mypy warnings in the codebase 
that could be cleaned up with minimal `type: ignore` comments.

## Current State

Running mypy on latest main (commit 0771efc5a0) shows:
```
pandas\core\arrays\datetimes.py:2973: error: Non-overlapping identity check 
(left operand type: "Timestamp", right operand type: "NaTType")
pandas\core\arrays\datetimes.py:2981: error: Non-overlapping identity check 
(left operand type: "Timestamp", right operand type: "NaTType")
```

## Proposed Solution

Add `# type: ignore[comparison-overlap]` comments to these specific lines:
```python
# Line 2973
if start is not NaT:  # type: ignore[comparison-overlap]
    start = start.as_unit(unit)

# Line 2981  
if end is not NaT:  # type: ignore[comparison-overlap]
    end = end.as_unit(unit)
```
## Alternatives Considered
I considered using `typing.cast(object, start)` to make the check valid, but `type: ignore` seemed less verbose for a known false positive. I am happy to implement whichever pattern the team prefers.
## Context

This is NOT proposing to reopen #58475 or implement the rejected constructors. 
This is simply cleaning up the expected mypy warnings that result from the 
team's decision to keep the current type system.

## Environment
- pandas: 2.3.0.dev0+1847.g0771efc5a0
- Python: 3.14.0
- mypy: 1.19.1

I'm happy to submit a PR if this approach is acceptable.

title: BUG: `pd.read_spss()` generates `attrs` that cause `DataFrame.to_parquet` to crash when generating JSON metadata.
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

``` sh 
pip install pandas pyreadstat
```

``` python
import pandas as pd
import pyreadstat

source_df = pd.DataFrame([[1,2.0,"a"],[3,4.0,"b"]], columns=["v1", "v2", "v3"])
column_labels = ["Variable 1", "Variable 2", "Variable 3"]
pyreadstat.write_sav(source_df, "spss_data.sav", file_label="test", column_labels=column_labels)

read_df = pd.read_spss("spss_data.sav")
print(read_df.attrs) # contains creation_time and modification_time keys with datetime values
# read_df.attrs.clear() # enabling this line allows parquet writing to succeed
read_df.to_parquet("spss_data.parquet") # crashes
```

### Issue Description

Possibly not strictly a pandas bug, possibly pyarrow, possibly pyreadstat, but pandas is the project linking it all together.

Pandas leans on pyreadstat to process spss files and pyarrow to write parquet files.

pyreadstat generates a metadata dictionary which pandas assigns to `attrs` in `pandas.io.spss.read_spss`. This dict contains `creation_time` and `modification_time` keys of `datetime.datetime`, which crash json.dumps when metadata is created from `attrs` during writing of a parquet file in `pyarrow.pandas_compat.construct_metadata`.

### Expected Behavior

Parquet writing should succeed for a dataframe created from an spss file.

title: ENH: `Timestamp.round`: officially accept `Timedelta` arguments
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

`Timestamp.round` should accept arbitrary `Timedelta`, so that we don't need to stringify types.

This actually already works at runtime, because internally [`Timestamp.round`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Timestamp.round.html) parses the `freq` argument with [`pandas.tseries.frequencies.to_offset`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.tseries.frequencies.to_offset.html) but it is not documented:

```python
import pandas as pd

freq = "1h30min"
offset = pd.Timedelta(freq)

dt = pd.Timestamp.now()
dt.round(freq)  # ✅️ (documented)
dt.round(offset)  # ✅️ (undocumented)
dt.round(str(offset)) # ❌️ fails
```

If accepted, one should also consider patching `pandas.tseries.frequencies.to_offset` so that it gives identical results when passing a `Timedelta` versus casting that timedelta to string. In fact, it seems like internally it should probably just cast the string to timedelta first before processing it further.


### Feature Description

1. Update documentation / type-hints of `Timestamp.round` to allow `Timedelta` argument
2. (Optional): update `pandas.tseries.frequencies.to_offset` so that `to_offset(string_argument)` and `to_offset(str(Timedelta(string_argument)))` always give identical results.

title: BUG: data races when simultaneously reading data frames in multiple threads
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import threading

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from io import StringIO
from textwrap import dedent

import numpy as np

from pandas import read_csv

# From statsmodels.datasets.longley
longley_csv = StringIO(
    dedent(
        """"Obs","GNPDEFL","GNP","UNEMP","ARMED","POP","YEAR"
        1,83,234289,2356,1590,107608,1947
        2,88.5,259426,2325,1456,108632,1948
        3,88.2,258054,3682,1616,109773,1949
        4,89.5,284599,3351,1650,110929,1950
        5,96.2,328975,2099,3099,112075,1951
        6,98.1,346999,1932,3594,113270,1952
        7,99,365385,1870,3547,115094,1953
        8,100,363112,3578,3350,116219,1954
        9,101.2,397469,2904,3048,117388,1955
        10,104.6,419180,2822,2857,118734,1956
        11,108.4,442769,2936,2798,120445,1957
        12,110.8,444546,4681,2637,121950,1958
        13,112.6,482704,3813,2552,123366,1959
        14,114.2,502601,3931,2514,125368,1960
        15,115.7,518173,4806,2572,127852,1961
        16,116.9,554894,4007,2827,130081,1962
        """
    )
)

data = read_csv(longley_csv).iloc[:, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]].astype(float)

n_threads = 4
b = threading.Barrier(n_threads)


def closure():
    b.wait()
    np.testing.assert_array_equal(data, data)

with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=n_threads) as tpe:
    futures = [tpe.submit(closure) for _ in range(n_threads)]
    [f.result() for f in futures]
```

### Issue Description

@kumaraditya303 originally discovered this issue working on free-threaded support for statsmodels, running their test suite under [pytest-run-parallel](https://github.com/Quansight-Labs/pytest-run-parallel) - a pytest plugin that runs tests repeatedly in a thread pool to shake out thread safety issues.

I built pandas and all dependencies, including CPython, using thread sanitizer. See https://py-free-threading.github.io/thread_sanitizer/ for more about using thread sanitizer with Python projects. An annoying aspect of this is that you need to use the same compiler stack to compile everything. On a Mac it's kind of complicated to set this up for Pandas because of the dependency on SciPy, which needs OpenMP, which also means you can't use the Apple clang compilers to build everything. I shared instructions for doing this on the [issue tracker our team uses to track ecosystem issues on the free-threaded build](https://github.com/Quansight-Labs/free-threaded-compatibility/issues/309).

You may have to run the script repeatedly in a loop to see it. How likely the race is depends on CPU timing so different machines may not hit this. I'm testing on an M3 Pro Macbook Pro.

The issue in this race is that the implementation of `_ensure_mapping_populated` isn't thread safe:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/ff0cd9a3a7d5d29344be7fb26aa457ce32763ad0/pandas/_libs/index.pyx#L347-L356

In addition, I've also seen races in cases that involve mutating a dataframe generating the `_as_array` attribute of `BlockPlacement`, which isn't thread-safe:

https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/14dbf0575f903070da65bfa1202b0e064fa0d711/pandas/_libs/internals.pyx#L146-L153

@kumaraditya303 also saw races in the `BlockManager` implementation:

- [get_slice](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/14dbf0575f903070da65bfa1202b0e064fa0d711/pandas/_libs/internals.pyx#L879-L892):
  The assignment of `_blknos` in _slice_mgr_rows is not thread safe
- [_rebuild_blknos_and_blklocs](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/14dbf0575f903070da65bfa1202b0e064fa0d711/pandas/_libs/internals.pyx#L762C11-L762C38):
  This does lazy initialization of `_blknos` which is not thread safe
- _ensure_has_slice: Called from a number of places and lazily initializes `_as_slice` which is not thread safe

I think for all of these patterns, Pandas should be using a low-level single-initialization API that ensures only one thread can populate these lazy attributes: https://cython.readthedocs.io/en/latest/src/userguide/freethreading.html#use-c-for-low-level-synchronization-primitives. It might require using C++ mode in Cython to be able to use the C++ standard library. Unfortunately MSVC support for C standard library threading primitives is very recent and probably can't be relied on in general yet.

No data races reported by TSan.

title: BUG: pd.to_numeric Segmentation fault
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example (Updated)

I have managed to isolate the issue to a minimal reproducible example. Any scientific notation string where the exponent causes a 32-bit signed integer overflow (wrapping to negative) triggers the crash.

```python
import pandas as pd

# The exponent '3000000000' (3 billion) exceeds INT_MAX (2.14 billion)
# but is within the parser's digit limit (max_digits=17).
# This causes an integer overflow in the C parser.
s = pd.Series(["1E3000000000"])

print(f"Pandas version: {pd.__version__}")
print("Attempting to crash...")

# This triggers SIGSEGV immediately
res = pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce')
print(res)
```

### Issue Description
The Python interpreter crashes with a **Segmentation Fault (SIGSEGV)** when parsing specific strings that look like scientific notation.

The crash occurs in `precise_xstrtod` within `pandas/_libs/pandas_parser`.

### Root Cause Analysis

Based on the GDB trace and source code analysis, this is a **Signed Integer Overflow leading to an Out-of-Bounds Read**.

1.  **Integer Overflow**:
    In `precise_xstrtod` (tokenizer.c), the variable `n` (used to parse the exponent) is typically declared as `int` (32-bit signed).
    The input exponent `3000000000` is parsed. Since this exceeds `INT_MAX` (2,147,483,647), it overflows and is interpreted as a **negative number** (specifically `-1294967296` in 32-bit representation).

2.  **Bypassing Bounds Checks**:
    The code likely contains checks like `if (exponent > 308)`. Since the overflowed exponent is now negative, it bypasses this check and enters the logic path intended for small numbers (negative exponents).

3.  **Out-of-Bounds Read**:
    The code attempts to look up the power of 10 in the `static double e[]` array (size ~309).
    It calculates the index based on the corrupted negative exponent (e.g., accessing `e[-exponent]`). Since `-exponent` becomes a massive positive integer (approx 1.29 billion), it attempts to access invalid memory far beyond the array bounds.

    ```c
    // Pseudo-code logic failure
    } else {
       // exponent is negative due to overflow, so -exponent is huge positive
       number /= e[-exponent]; // CRASH: Index out of bounds
    }
    ```


### Installed Versions

2.3.3+8.gf18f394430, the latest from 2.3.x branch, besides, the 2.3.3 from pypi also crashes. 

Main branch (3.0rc1) works well without crash

title: BUG: Missing explicit libm dependency in meson.build causes undefined symbol errors
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
# Build pandas from source
pip install -v -v -v --compile --no-deps --no-cache-dir --no-build-isolation --no-binary :all: .

# Check for undefined symbols
find /usr/local/lib/python*/site-packages/pandas -name "*.so" -exec ldd -r -d {} \; 2>&1 | grep -i "undefined symbol"
```

### Issue Description

Several pandas C extension modules use math functions from `libm` (like `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, etc.) but don't explicitly declare the dependency in their `meson.build` files. This causes undefined symbol errors when building from source, particularly in minimal environments or when using certain toolchains.

Running `ldd -r -d` on the built extension modules shows undefined symbols for math functions. For example:

```bash
find /usr/local/lib/python*/site-packages/pandas -name "*.so" -exec ldd -r -d {} \; 2>&1 | grep -i "undefined symbol" || echo "No undefined symbols found"
```

This affects at least the following modules:
- `algos`
- `groupby`
- `sparse`
- `json`
- `conversion` (in tslibs)

### Proposed Solution

Add explicit `libm` dependency to the affected extension modules in the meson.build files.

1. Declare the libm dependency:
```meson
cc = meson.get_compiler('c')
m_dep = cc.find_library('m', required: true)
```

2. Add `m_dep` to the dependencies of affected modules:
```meson
'algos': {
    'sources': ['algos.pyx', _algos_common_helper, _algos_take_helper],
    'deps': [_khash_primitive_helper_dep, m_dep],  # Add m_dep
},
'groupby': {'sources': ['groupby.pyx'], 'deps': [m_dep]},
'sparse': {'sources': ['sparse.pyx', _sparse_op_helper], 'deps': [m_dep]},
'json': {
    'sources': [
        'src/vendored/ujson/python/ujson.c',
        'src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c',
        'src/vendored/ujson/python/JSONtoObj.c',
        'src/vendored/ujson/lib/ultrajsonenc.c',
        'src/vendored/ujson/lib/ultrajsondec.c'
    ],
    'deps': [m_dep]
},
```

Changes needed in `pandas/_libs/tslibs/meson.build`:

1. Declare the libm dependency at the top of the file
2. Add to conversion module:
```meson
'conversion': {'sources': ['conversion.pyx'], 'deps': [m_dep]},
```

### Expected Behavior

All C extensions that use math functions should explicitly link against `libm` to ensure symbols are properly resolved.

As a workaround, patch the necessary changes:

```bash
PANDAS_LIBM_MESON_BUILD_FILE_PATH="./pandas/_libs/meson.build"
PANDAS_LIBM_TSLIBS_MESON_BUILD_FILE_PATH="./pandas/_libs/tslibs/meson.build"

# 1. Add m_dep declaration before subdir('tslibs')
sed -i "/^subdir('tslibs')/i\\
cc = meson.get_compiler('c')\\
m_dep = cc.find_library('m', required: true)\\
" "${PANDAS_LIBM_MESON_BUILD_FILE_PATH}"

# 2. Add m_dep to algos (already has deps, convert to list and add m_dep)
sed -i "/^    'algos':/s/'deps': _khash_primitive_helper_dep/'deps': [_khash_primitive_helper_dep, m_dep]/" "${PANDAS_LIBM_MESON_BUILD_FILE_PATH}"

# 3. Add deps with m_dep to groupby (no existing deps)
sed -i "/^    'groupby':/s/},/, 'deps': [m_dep]},/" "${PANDAS_LIBM_MESON_BUILD_FILE_PATH}"

# 4. Add deps with m_dep to sparse (no existing deps)
sed -i "/^    'sparse':/s/},/, 'deps': [m_dep]},/" "${PANDAS_LIBM_MESON_BUILD_FILE_PATH}"

# 5. Add deps with m_dep to json (multi-line entry)
sed -i "/^    'json':/,/]},/{s/]},/], 'deps': [m_dep]},/}" "${PANDAS_LIBM_MESON_BUILD_FILE_PATH}"

# 6. Add m_dep declaration to tslibs/meson.build (at start of file)
```

title: ENH: Create `.rdiff()`, like `.diff()` but reversed, like `.rsub()` and `.sub()`
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas
- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas
- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Firstly, it's easy enough to get the behaviour I want by using other methods, so this is just a suggestion if you want it. By all means ignore if it would be more effort than it's worth. Hopefully it has non-trivial uses, but I can't think of any :P

I wanted to find gaps in a Series of integers, similar to [this SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/q/66021881/4518341 "How to detect gaps between integer sequence in pandas?"). All the answers use some variation of `s.shift(-1) - s - 1`, so I thought, it'd be more elegant to write that using `Series.diff`, but if you do `.diff(-1)`, you get negatives (when the Series is sorted ascending), so you have to invert it after: `s.diff(-1)*-1 - 1`. Or you can do `.diff(1).shift(-1)`.

What would be cleaner is to have a method `.rdiff()` that does the equivalent of `s.shift(-1) - s`, which I guess you could call the "reverse difference". As a bonus, this would create a symmetry: `.diff()` and `.rdiff()` like `.sub()` (subtract) and `.rsub()` (reversed subtract - or "reflected" subtract [according to the Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__rsub__)).

### Feature Description

If `x.diff(n)` does the equivalent of `x - x.shift(n)`, `x.rdiff(n)` does the equivalent of `x.shift(-n) - x`.

In actual fact, [`Series.diff` uses `algorithms.diff`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/9c8bc3e55188c8aff37207a74f1dd144980b8874/pandas/core/series.py#L3134C1-L3134C56), which [gets pretty complicated](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/9c8bc3e55188c8aff37207a74f1dd144980b8874/pandas/core/algorithms.py#L1339), so I'm glossing over the details.

### Alternative Solutions

As said above, this is easy enough to accomplish using other methods.

title: ENH: Add .center() method to DataFrame/Series for inspecting middle rows.
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I wish I could use pandas to inspect the middle rows of a DataFrame or Series using a simple method like .center(), analogous to .head() and .tail().

### Feature Description

def center(self, n: int = 5):
    """
    Return the middle n rows.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    n : int, default 5
        Number of rows to select.
    
    Returns
    -------
    type of caller
        The subset of the DataFrame or Series.
    """
    total_len = len(self)
    
    # Edge case: If the requested window is larger than the data, return the whole object
    # (consistent with .head() and .tail() behavior)
    if n >= total_len:
        return self
    
    # Calculate the middle index
    mid_idx = total_len // 2
    
    # Determine start index (integer division handles odd/even n automatically)
    start = max(0, mid_idx - (n // 2))
    
    # Determine end index
    end = start + n
    
    return self.iloc[start:end]


### Alternative Solutions

# Manual slicing with iloc
mid = len(df) // 2
df.iloc[mid - 2 : mid + 3]


### Additional Context


This feature addresses a gap in the API symmetry. head() allows inspection of the start, and tail() allows inspection of the end. center() would complete the inspection triad, making it intuitive to check the interior of the dataframe without leaving the method-chaining syntax.

title: ENH: Decay-weighted rolling aggregations with defined behavior for duplicate timestamps
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

Pandas provides rolling and time-based window aggregations for time-indexed data, but there is currently no built-in way to compute decay-weighted aggregations (e.g. exponential time decay) with well-defined behavior under irregular sampling and duplicate timestamps.

In practical datasets such as event logs, financial transactions, or sensor bursts, multiple observations may share the same timestamp, and users often want recent observations to contribute more heavily via a decay function rather than a fixed window cutoff.

Today, users typically work around this by:
 manually computing weights and applying `groupby` + `apply`
 resampling or reindexing to a regular grid (which can distort the data)
 using ad-hoc NumPy logic outside pandas

These approaches are error-prone, slow, and lack consistent semantics for ties and normalization.


### Feature Description

This issue proposes discussing support for decay-weighted rolling aggregations over time-indexed data, where weights are a function of time distance rather than observation order.

Key aspects to clarify include:
 How decay functions (e.g. exponential) should be parameterized in time units
 How duplicate timestamps ("ties") should be aggregated before or during weighting
 How normalization should behave when windows contain sparse or coincident observations
 Whether this should extend existing `rolling` APIs or be introduced as a new aggregation mechanism

At a high level, the goal would be to define consistent, well-documented semantics rather than immediately finalize an API.

If this direction aligns with pandas’ design principles, I would be happy to prototype or iterate on an implementation based on maintainer feedback.


### Alternative Solutions

Current workarounds include manually computing decay weights and using `groupby` + `apply`, resampling irregular data to a fixed frequency, or exporting data to NumPy/SciPy and re-importing the results. These approaches work in some cases but tend to be verbose, error-prone, and inconsistent, especially when dealing with irregular sampling or duplicate timestamps.

Pandas’ existing `ewm` methods cover exponential weighting based on observation order, but they don’t directly address time-based decay on irregular time indexes or define behavior for coincident timestamps in rolling/windowed contexts.

title: BUG: pd.Grouper converts PyArrow timestamp to numpy datetime64
body:
### Pandas version checks

- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.


### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd
import io

data = '''agency_cd,site_no,datetime,tz_cd,144166_00060,144166_00060_cd,144167_00065,144167_00065_cd
USGS,9333500,2001-05-07 01:00:00,MDT,71.0,A:[91],,
USGS,9333500,2001-05-07 01:15:00,MDT,71.0,A:[91],,
USGS,9333500,2001-05-07 01:30:00,MDT,71.0,A:[91],,
USGS,9333500,2001-05-07 01:45:00,MDT,70.0,A:[91],,
USGS,9333500,2001-05-07 02:00:00,MDT,70.0,A:[91],,
USGS,9333500,2001-05-08 02:15:00,MDT,69.0,A:[91],,
USGS,9333500,2001-05-08 02:30:00,MDT,70.0,A:[91],,
USGS,9333500,2001-05-08 02:45:00,MDT,70.0,A:[91],,
USGS,9333500,2001-05-08 03:00:00,MDT,70.0,A:[91],,'''

df = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO(data), dtype_backend='pyarrow', engine='pyarrow')

def to_denver_time(df_, time_col, tz_col):
    return (df_
     .assign(**{tz_col: df_[tz_col].replace('MDT', 'MST7MDT')})
     .groupby(tz_col)
     [time_col]
     .transform(lambda s: pd.to_datetime(s)
         .dt.tz_localize(s.name, ambiguous=True)
         .dt.tz_convert('America/Denver'))
     .astype('timestamp[ns, America/Denver][pyarrow]')
    )

def tweak_river(df_):
    return (df_
     .assign(datetime=to_denver_time(df_, 'datetime', 'tz_cd'))
     .rename(columns={'144166_00060': 'cfs'})
     .loc[:, ['datetime', 'cfs']]
     .set_index('datetime')
    )

dd = tweak_river(df)

# Check the dtype before grouping
print("Before pd.Grouper:")
print(f"Index dtype: {dd.index.dtype}")

# Use pd.Grouper to group by day
result = dd.groupby(pd.Grouper(freq='D')).median(numeric_only=True)

# Check the dtype after grouping
print("\nAfter pd.Grouper:")
print(f"Index dtype: {result.index.dtype}")
```

### Issue Description

When using `pd.Grouper` with a PyArrow-backed timestamp column, the resulting index is automatically converted from the PyArrow dtype (`timestamp[ns, America/Denver][pyarrow]`) to the numpy-backed dtype (`datetime64[ns, America/Denver]`). This conversion happens silently and is inconsistent with the goal of maintaining PyArrow types throughout the analysis pipeline.

This affects users working with PyArrow backend who want to maintain PyArrow types for performance and consistency reasons.

### Expected Behavior

The resulting index after using `pd.Grouper` should maintain the original PyArrow dtype (`timestamp[ns, America/Denver][pyarrow]`) instead of converting to numpy's `datetime64[ns, America/Denver]`.

title: ENH: Add an opt in operation report for time memory and copy behavior
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas

- [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas

- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas


### Problem Description

I want a reliable way to understand why a single pandas operation is slow or uses far more memory than I expect. When a merge, groupby, sort, or rolling call suddenly takes minutes or crashes with out of memory, pandas completes the work or fails without telling me what path it took, how many temporary arrays were created, or where the time went. That leaves me guessing, rewriting code, and trying different dtypes and arguments until something improves.

External profilers can show Python level hotspots, but they do not answer the pandas specific questions I need in the moment. I need something that can tell me whether a join built a large hash table, whether groupby spent most of its time building the grouper, whether a sort triggered large copies, and whether Copy on Write forced unexpected materialization. With that information I could make simple changes like adjusting key dtypes, choosing observed or sort settings, reducing columns earlier, or validating join cardinality. Without it, debugging performance and memory spikes is slow, fragile, and hard to reproduce.

### Feature Description

A practical way to build this is to introduce an opt in collector that wraps a single pandas operation and produces a compact report. When diagnostics are turned off, nothing happens apart from one cheap check, so there is no meaningful overhead in normal use.

The public entry point can be pd.diagnostics.report(func, *args, **kwargs) with an optional context manager for the same behavior. Internally, the wrapper sets a thread local reference to the active collector, starts wall time measurement and optional memory tracking, executes the operation, then stops tracking and clears the thread local. After the call completes, the collector freezes the captured metrics into a DiagnosticsReport object, which is attached to the returned result via a private attribute. A public DataFrame.explain() method can then format that report as text or json.

On the pandas internals side, the only required plumbing is a small helper such as pd.diagnostics._collector() that returns None when diagnostics are disabled. Hot paths can call this helper and, when it is present, record a few coarse phases using begin and end markers, plus counts for allocations and copies at places where pandas already allocates new arrays or forces a copy. Instrumentation can start with merge, groupby, sort, and rolling. Memory reporting can rely on tracemalloc as a best effort estimate and remain optional because it adds overhead.

### Alternative Solutions

Today the closest options are general purpose profilers and memory tools. We can time operations with timeit or perf_counter, profile CPU with cProfile or py spy, and track allocations with tracemalloc or external packages like memory profiler or scalene. These tools are useful, but they are not pandas aware, so they do not explain which internal path was taken, how many intermediate arrays were created, or what simple argument and dtype changes would help.

Pandas itself offers pieces like DataFrame.info() and memory_usage() plus performance guidance in the docs, and merge validation can catch some join blowups early, but none of these provide an on demand structured report for a single operation.

### Additional Context

The idea was basically from other existing frameworks. For e.g. Apache Spark has a built in DataFrame.explain(), polars has LazyFrame.explain(), duckdb has  EXPLAIN, etc. 

Please let me know if the idea sounds good, i can dedicate some time and start working on the PR.

Like .sample() but the data returned is contiguous, in essence the method randomly samples 1 row idx and then samples the next N from that point.

### Feature Description

Add a contiguous param to .sample or create a new .sample_contgiuous

Draw from distribution a single idx

and select N around that as a contiguous block

### Alternative Solutions

def random_contiguous_sample(df, n):
    max_start = len(df) - n

    start_idx = np.random.randint(0, max_start + 1)
    return df.iloc[start_idx:start_idx + n]

title: API: comparing time series with index of different unit should work
body:
Taking the example from https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63417, but opening a separate issue to focus on just the behaviour with mismatching unit, regardless of performance issues.

pandas generally aligns on the index in all operations, _except_ for comparison operations, where we raise an error for mis-aligned indices (_"Can only compare identically-labeled Series objects"_). 

But currently, two DatetimeIndex with the same values but different unit is apparently considered as "not identical", and thus you get errors like this:

```python
dti = pd.date_range("2016-01-01", periods=3)
ser = pd.Series(1, index=dti)
ser2 = pd.Series(1, index=dti.as_unit("ns"))

>>> ser == ser2
...
File ~/scipy/repos/pandas/pandas/core/series.py:6656, in Series._cmp_method(self, other, op)
   6653 res_name = ops.get_op_result_name(self, other)
   6655 if isinstance(other, Series) and not self._indexed_same(other):
-> 6656     raise ValueError("Can only compare identically-labeled Series objects")
   6658 lvalues = self._values
   6659 rvalues = extract_array(other, extract_numpy=True, extract_range=True)

ValueError: Can only compare identically-labeled Series objects
```

With pandas 3.0, since we now no longer default to nanoseconds in all cases (typically microseconds, but also other resolutions depending on how you created the timestamp data), I assume this would be more common. 

And generally, my feeling is that the above comparison should Just Work?

cc @pandas-dev/pandas-core

### Reproducible Example

```python
import pandas as pd

pd.Series(1).min()         # works
pd.Series().min()          # works
 
pd.Series(1).abs()         # works
pd.Series().abs()          # works
```

```
        nv.validate_round(args, kwargs)
        if self.dtype == "object":
>           raise TypeError("Expected numeric dtype, got object instead.")
E           TypeError: Expected numeric dtype, got object instead.

.../lib/python3.13/site-packages/pandas/core/series.py:2821: TypeError
```

^ not a very helpful error either when you don't have access to the DataFrame that caused it. 

### Issue Description

Pandas functions gracefully handle an empty Series/DataFrame, except for `round()`, which seems to be an exception.
I have the following code that incorporates other operations (cumsum, shift, division) that don't fail on an empty DataFrame `filter_stats`:

```python
        filter_stats["requests_available"] = requests_available
        filter_stats["requests_available"] -= \
            filter_stats["blocked_requests"].cumsum().shift(1).fillna(0)
        filter_stats["blocked_percentage"] = \
            (filter_stats["blocked_requests"] / filter_stats["requests_available"] * 100)
```
but the moment you add a round, it fails on the empty `filter_stats`:
```python
        filter_stats["requests_available"] = requests_available
        filter_stats["requests_available"] -= \
            filter_stats["blocked_requests"].cumsum().shift(1).fillna(0)
        filter_stats["blocked_percentage"] = \
            (filter_stats["blocked_requests"] / filter_stats["requests_available"] * 100).round(4)
```

This creates an unexpected edge case because it only exists using `round()`.

### Expected Behavior

`round()` should handle empty Series gracefully, without erroring out, returning an empty Series. 
In alignment with other similar functions.

title: API: read_json should follow general default of microseconds
body:
`pd.read_json` still returns nanoseconds always:

```python
>>> df = pd.DataFrame({"col": range(5), "dates": pd.date_range("2025", periods=5)})
>>> s = df.to_json(date_format="iso")
>>> pd.read_json(io.StringIO(s), convert_dates=["dates"]).dtypes
col               int64
dates    datetime64[ns]
dtype: object
```

Since JSON is a format like CSV that has no type / unit information stored, we should follow the general default of microseconds (or nanoseconds if those are present), like we do for CSV (or HTML, XML, excel, etc)

title: ENH: Add read/write support for the Vortex columnar format
body:
### Feature Type

- [x] Adding new functionality to pandas
- [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas
- [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas

### Problem Description

Pandas currently has no way to read or write data in the Vortex format (https://lf-ai.github.io/vortex/), a new open columnar storage format developed under the Linux Foundation. As Vortex adoption grows, pandas users cannot easily load these datasets without first converting them to Parquet or Arrow, adding unnecessary steps and limiting interoperability.

### Feature Description

Add optional pandas IO support for Vortex, similar to existing Parquet and Arrow readers/writers. This could include:

- `pd.read_vortex(path, **kwargs)`
- `DataFrame.to_vortex(path, **kwargs)`

Support may rely on a Python Vortex library or an Arrow-based bridge if one becomes available.

### Alternative Solutions

- Convert Vortex → Parquet or Arrow → pandas
- Use custom Python wrappers
- Switch to other DataFrame libraries that add Vortex support

These options work but are less efficient and not user-friendly.

### Additional Context

Vortex is designed for high-performance, compressed, columnar analytics and aligns well with Arrow-style data workflows. Native pandas interoperability would make it easier for the Python ecosystem to evaluate and adopt the format.

title: Constructor with invalid unicode: automatically fall back to object dtype?
body:
We documented that invalid unicode can no longer be stored in a `str` dtype column (https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/user_guide/migration-3-strings.html#invalid-unicode-input), and for sure that will error when you explicitly ask for `str`:

```python
>>> pd.Series(['\ud800'], dtype=str)
...
UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\ud800' in position 0: surrogates not allowed
```

But I am wondering if we should still by default fall back to object dtype in the case you are not specifying a dtype, i.e. for the default inference. Right now also `pd.Series(['\ud800'])` gives the same error. 
(it might be a performance cost in validating that up front though, or otherwise we could the specific error if we know we started without user-specified dtype)
